<style>
  :root{
    /* Canonical brand tokens — PlotNua Brand Package v1.0. Do not alter. */
    --brand-green:#1F3B2E; --brand-ivory:#F2EFE6; --brand-sage:#8FAF8A;
    --cream:#F2EFE6; --paper:#F8F5EC; --ink:#1F3B2E; --soft:#55605A;
    --accent:#4F6B4A; --oak:#8B6F4E;
  }
  *{box-sizing:border-box; margin:0; padding:0;}
  html{scroll-behavior:smooth;}
  body{ font-family:'Work Sans',sans-serif; background:var(--paper); color:var(--ink); overflow-x:hidden; }
  h1,h2,h3{ font-family:'Fraunces',serif; font-weight:600; letter-spacing:-.01em; }
  h1,h2{ font-weight:700; }

  .reveal{ opacity:0; transform:translateY(6px); transition:opacity 1.1s ease, transform 1.1s ease; }
  .reveal.in{ opacity:1; transform:none; }

  /* ---- fixed brand mark (unchanged from Brand Integration v1) ---- */
  .brand-mark{
    position:fixed; top:22px; left:22px; z-index:50;
    display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:center;
    width:46px; height:46px; padding:0;
    background:var(--brand-ivory);
    border-radius:12px;
    box-shadow:0 1px 3px rgba(31,59,46,.16), 0 0 0 1px rgba(31,59,46,.07);
    opacity:0; transition:opacity 1.6s ease, transform .4s cubic-bezier(.4,0,.2,1), box-shadow .4s ease;
    text-decoration:none;
  }
  .brand-mark:hover{ transform:scale(1.06); box-shadow:0 5px 16px rgba(31,59,46,.20), 0 0 0 1px rgba(31,59,46,.09); }

  /* RESULTS-003 PART D — THE FLOATING BACK.
     Identical to the control on Results and My Plot: same corner, same 44px
     minimum height, same radius, paper ground, hairline border and shadow,
     same type. Only the label and destination differ, because they must.

     It does not fight the brand mark. Measured: .brand-mark is fixed at
     TOP:22px left:22px, this is fixed at BOTTOM:22px left:22px. Opposite
     ends of the screen at every viewport. (I twice deferred this work on the
     stated grounds that they shared a corner. They never did.)

     z-index 60 sits above the page and below .am-modal-overlay (200), so an
     open modal covers it rather than having it float over a dialog. */
  .pn-return{
    position:fixed; left:22px; bottom:22px; z-index:60;
    display:inline-flex; align-items:center; gap:8px;
    min-height:44px; padding:11px 17px 11px 14px;
    background:var(--paper, #F8F5EC); color:var(--ink, #1F3B2E);
    border:1px solid rgba(31,59,46,.16); border-radius:24px;
    box-shadow:0 2px 10px rgba(31,59,46,.13);
    font-family:'Work Sans',sans-serif; font-size:14px; font-weight:500;
    text-decoration:none; cursor:pointer;
    -webkit-appearance:none; appearance:none;
  }
  .pn-return:hover{ border-color:rgba(31,59,46,.3); }
  .pn-return-arrow{ font-size:15px; line-height:1; }
  @media (max-width:600px){
    .pn-return{ left:16px; bottom:16px; padding:10px 15px 10px 12px; font-size:13.5px; }
  }
  .brand-mark.in{ opacity:1; }
  .brand-mark img{ display:block; width:34px; height:34px; border-radius:8px; }
  @media(max-width:720px){
    .brand-mark{ top:16px; left:16px; width:40px; height:40px; }
    .brand-mark img{ width:30px; height:30px; }
  }

  /* ================= DISCOVERY — HERO =================
     Same visual grammar as the About page hero: a single still image,
     bottom-anchored copy, warm ivory serif type. This is the master
     template every future Discovery reuses, so the hero deliberately
     stays close to the About page's pattern rather than inventing a
     new one — consistency here is what makes the site feel like one
     continuous place, not a stitched-together set of templates. */
  .d-hero{ position:relative; width:100%; height:88vh; height:88svh; min-height:540px; overflow:hidden; background:var(--ink); }
  .d-hero img{
    width:100%; height:100%; object-fit:cover; display:block;
    transform:scale(1.03); opacity:0;
    transition:opacity 1.8s ease-out, transform 6s cubic-bezier(.22,.61,.36,1);
  }
  .d-hero img.on{ opacity:1; transform:scale(1); }
  .d-hero-scrim{ position:absolute; inset:0;
    background:linear-gradient(180deg, rgba(15,14,10,.14) 0%, rgba(15,14,10,0) 32%, rgba(15,14,10,.10) 60%, rgba(15,14,10,.60) 100%); }
  .d-hero-scrim{ background:linear-gradient(180deg,
    rgba(15,14,10,.16) 0%, rgba(15,14,10,0) 26%,
    rgba(15,14,10,.42) 58%, rgba(15,14,10,.78) 100%); }
  .d-hero-copy{ position:absolute; z-index:2; inset:auto 0 0 0; padding:0 8vw 10vh; text-align:center; }
  /* HERO EYEBROW — ADAPTIVE COLOUR (Master Standard).
     The eyebrow is an orientation label, not a brand element. On this hero
     --brand-sage (luminance 0.36) sat inside the luminance range of the
     plaster wall behind it (0.32-0.49) and washed out; no shadow can
     separate a colour from a background it matches in lightness.
     It therefore uses the same --brand-ivory as h1 / .subtitle / .intro,
     with the same shadow family as .intro. Font, size, weight, tracking
     and position are unchanged. */
  .d-hero-copy .eyebrow{ opacity:0; transform:translateY(10px); transition:opacity 1s ease, transform 1s ease;
    font-size:12px; letter-spacing:.18em; text-transform:uppercase; color:var(--brand-ivory); margin-bottom:20px;
    text-shadow:0 1px 14px rgba(0,0,0,.28); }
  .d-hero-copy h1{ opacity:0; transform:translateY(10px); transition:opacity 1s ease .1s, transform 1s ease .1s;
    color:var(--brand-ivory); font-size:clamp(32px,5vw,58px); line-height:1.14; text-shadow:0 2px 24px rgba(0,0,0,.32); }
  .d-hero-copy .subtitle{ opacity:0; transform:translateY(10px); transition:opacity 1s ease .18s, transform 1s ease .18s;
    margin:18px auto 0; max-width:32ch; font-family:'Fraunces',serif; font-style:italic; font-weight:400;
    color:var(--brand-ivory); font-size:clamp(16px,1.9vw,21px); line-height:1.55; text-shadow:0 1px 16px rgba(0,0,0,.3); }
  .d-hero-copy .intro{ opacity:0; transform:translateY(10px); transition:opacity 1s ease .26s, transform 1s ease .26s;
    margin:24px auto 0; max-width:50ch; font-family:'Work Sans',sans-serif; font-weight:300;
    color:var(--brand-ivory); font-size:clamp(14px,1.4vw,16px); line-height:1.75; text-shadow:0 1px 14px rgba(0,0,0,.28); }
  .d-hero-copy.in .eyebrow, .d-hero-copy.in h1, .d-hero-copy.in .subtitle{ opacity:1; transform:none; }
  .d-hero-copy.in .intro{ opacity:.86; transform:none; }

  /* ================= ARTICLE RHYTHM (shared with About) ================= */
  .article{ max-width:1040px; margin:0 auto; padding:0 7vw; }
  .article-section{ padding:9.5vh 0; border-bottom:1px solid rgba(31,59,46,.06); }
  .article-section:last-of-type{ border-bottom:none; }
  .article-section .kicker{ font-size:12px; letter-spacing:.16em; text-transform:uppercase; color:var(--accent); margin-bottom:19px; }
  .article-section h2{ font-size:clamp(26px,3.4vw,40px); line-height:1.32; max-width:19ch; margin-bottom:26px; }
  .article-section p{ color:var(--soft); font-size:17px; line-height:1.85; max-width:60ch; }
  .article-section p + p{ margin-top:20px; }

  /* ---- The Spark — the emotional opening line of every Discovery.
     Deliberately the quietest, largest moment on the page: one
     sentence, generous whitespace, nothing else competing with it. ---- */
  .spark{ position:relative; padding:12vh 7vw; text-align:center; background:var(--paper); overflow:hidden; }
  .spark::before{ content:''; position:absolute; top:0; left:0; right:0; height:16vh;
    background:linear-gradient(180deg, rgba(20,26,20,.05) 0%, rgba(20,26,20,0) 100%); pointer-events:none; }
  .spark p{ position:relative; font-family:'Fraunces',serif; font-style:italic; font-weight:400; color:var(--ink);
    font-size:clamp(25px,3.6vw,40px); line-height:1.5; max-width:21ch; margin:0 auto; letter-spacing:-.005em; }

  /* ---- Imagine Your Property — a second full-width photograph with
     minimal text; this is a mood beat, not an information beat. ---- */
  .imagine-photo{ position:relative; width:100%; height:84vh; height:84svh; min-height:460px; overflow:hidden; background:var(--ink); }
  .imagine-photo img{ width:100%; height:100%; object-fit:cover; display:block; }
  .imagine-photo::before, .imagine-photo::after{ content:''; position:absolute; left:0; right:0; height:5vh; z-index:2; pointer-events:none; }
  .imagine-photo::before{ top:0; background:linear-gradient(180deg, rgba(248,245,236,.5) 0%, rgba(248,245,236,0) 100%); }
  .imagine-photo::after{ bottom:0; background:linear-gradient(0deg, rgba(242,239,230,.5) 0%, rgba(242,239,230,0) 100%); }

  /* RULE 6 — the Discovery annotation, drawn over the plate rather than burned
     into the file. DISC-029 retires the older asset-classification wording: its
     cue is PLOTNUA DISCOVERY / What if the bins disappeared… The SVG uses the image's own aspect ratio and the same
     xMidYMid slice crop as object-fit:cover, so the anchor stays on the roof at
     every viewport. Everything sits inside the horizontal centre band so it
     survives the heavy side-crop on narrow screens. */
  /* The SEAI quotation and the Looking Ahead lede: this page is the first
     Discovery to need either, so both are defined here rather than remapped
     onto a class that means something else. */
  /* This is the first Discovery to use h3 as a subheading inside an article
     section, so the donor never needed a rule. Direct child only, so the FAQ
     h3s inside <summary> keep their own zero-margin treatment. */
  .article-section > h3{ margin:36px 0 12px; }

  .pull-quote{ margin:28px 0 24px; padding:2px 0 2px 22px; border-left:2px solid var(--brand-sage);
    font-family:'Fraunces',Georgia,serif; font-size:19px; line-height:1.66;
    color:var(--ink); max-width:56ch; }
  .quarantine-lede{ font-style:italic; color:var(--ink); max-width:56ch; margin-bottom:26px; }

  /* ---- RULE 6 — THE ANNOTATED FRAME IS THE WHOLE PLATE.

     An annotated plate is not an ordinary photograph. The photograph, the
     PLOTNUA DISCOVERY kicker, the Discovery cue, the wash, the leader and
     the dot are one composed explanatory graphic, and cropping any of it destroys
     the explanation rather than trimming a picture.

     The overlay shares the plate's coordinate system and is sliced with it, so it
     stays registered to the photograph. That is correct and must not change. What
     was wrong is that the FRAME was sized from the viewport (84vh, 62vh) rather
     than from the plate, so the plate was cropped and the annotation with it:
     measured, only the middle 42% of the plate survived at 390 and 50% at 768,
     and above 1354px the plate was still cropped top and bottom — which is what
     clipped DISC-006's label at 1920.

     The frame now takes its height from the plate at EVERY width. Nothing can be
     cropped, so there is no safe band to compose around on either axis, and a
     future Discovery inherits this by adding one class.

     Scoped to .pa-frame: unannotated plates keep the tall full-bleed frame.

     The caption and the edge gradients keep the site's existing 820px breakpoint,
     because a short band needs less of both. That is presentation. The height
     rule above it carries no breakpoint, because cropping is not presentation. ---- */
  .imagine-photo.pa-frame{ height:auto; min-height:0; }
  .imagine-photo.pa-frame img{ height:auto; }
  @media (max-width:820px){
    .imagine-photo.pa-frame::before,
    .imagine-photo.pa-frame::after{ height:18px; }
    .imagine-photo.pa-frame .caption{ padding:26px 8vw 20px; }
  }

  .pa-annot{ position:absolute; inset:0; z-index:3; pointer-events:none; }
  /* On the hero the annotation sits BENEATH the scrim and the copy,
     so the headline never reads through a wash. */
  .d-hero .pa-annot{ z-index:1; }
  .pa-annot svg{ width:100%; height:100%; display:block; }
  .pa-line{ stroke:rgba(15,14,10,.78); stroke-width:1.6; fill:none; }
  .pa-dot{ fill:none; stroke:rgba(15,14,10,.85); stroke-width:2.2; }
  .pa-wash{ fill:rgba(255,255,255,.60); }
  .pa-kicker{ font-family:'Work Sans',system-ui,sans-serif; font-size:15px; font-weight:500;
    letter-spacing:.18em; fill:rgba(15,14,10,.72); }
  .pa-label{ font-family:'Fraunces',Georgia,serif; font-style:italic; font-size:27px;
    fill:rgba(15,14,10,.92); }
  .imagine-photo .caption{ position:absolute; z-index:3; left:0; right:0; bottom:0; padding:7vh 8vw;
    background:linear-gradient(180deg, rgba(15,14,10,0) 0%, rgba(15,14,10,.42) 100%); text-align:center; }
  .imagine-photo .caption p{ font-family:'Fraunces',serif; font-style:italic; font-weight:400;
    color:var(--brand-ivory); font-size:clamp(16px,1.85vw,20px); max-width:32ch; margin:0 auto; text-shadow:0 1px 16px rgba(0,0,0,.3); letter-spacing:.01em; }

  /* ---- Could This Work For You — reflective questions, same
     fragment-line treatment used across the site for short phrases,
     given here as questions rather than statements. ---- */

  /* ---- Understanding the Opportunity — practical detail, still
     presented as prose rather than a spec sheet. Sub-headings stay
     small and quiet so the page never tips into "brochure." ---- */
  .practical-group{ margin-top:12px; }
  .practical-item{ padding:19px 0; border-top:1px solid rgba(31,59,46,.06); }
  .practical-item:first-child{ border-top:none; padding-top:0; }
  .practical-item h3{ font-size:clamp(18px,1.9vw,21px); margin-bottom:11px; }
  .practical-item p{ color:var(--soft); font-size:16px; line-height:1.8; max-width:56ch; }

  /* ---- Things To Consider — balanced points, same quiet list

  .considerations{ margin-top:10px; }
  .considerations p{ color:var(--soft); font-size:16px; line-height:1.85; max-width:58ch; margin-bottom:16px; }
  .considerations p:last-child{ margin-bottom:0; }

  /* ---- Trusted Partners — premium placeholder. Reads as a promise,
     not an empty state; no logos, no "coming soon" badge. ---- */
  .partners{ position:relative; background:var(--cream); }
  .partners::before{ content:''; position:absolute; top:0; left:0; right:0; height:10vh;
    background:linear-gradient(180deg, var(--paper) 0%, rgba(248,245,236,0) 100%); pointer-events:none; }
  .partners::after{ content:''; position:absolute; bottom:0; left:0; right:0; height:10vh;
    background:linear-gradient(0deg, var(--paper) 0%, rgba(248,245,236,0) 100%); pointer-events:none; }
  .partners .article{ position:relative; z-index:1; padding-top:12vh; padding-bottom:12vh; text-align:center; }
  .partners .kicker{ font-size:12px; letter-spacing:.16em; text-transform:uppercase; color:var(--soft); opacity:.8; margin-bottom:24px; }
  .partners h2{ max-width:none; margin:0 auto 20px; font-size:clamp(22px,2.6vw,30px); line-height:1.35; }
  .partners p{ margin:0 auto; max-width:52ch; }
  .partners .partner-frame{ margin:48px auto 0; max-width:420px; padding:38px 32px; border:1px solid rgba(31,59,46,.10); border-radius:2px; }
  .partners .partner-frame p{ font-family:'Fraunces',serif; font-style:italic; color:var(--accent); font-size:16px; line-height:1.75; max-width:none; }

  /* ---- inline links in body copy, carried from the launch standard ---- */
  .article-section p a, .planning-conditions a, .faq-a a{
    color:var(--accent); text-decoration:none;
    border-bottom:1px solid rgba(79,107,74,.35); padding-bottom:1px;
    transition:border-color .3s ease; }
  .article-section p a:hover, .planning-conditions a:hover, .faq-a a:hover{
    border-bottom-color:var(--accent); }

  /* ---- hand-off pair, as DISC-004 ---- */
  .handoff-pair{ margin-top:30px; display:flex; flex-direction:column; gap:14px; }
  .handoff{ padding:22px 26px 24px; background:var(--cream);
    border-left:2px solid var(--accent); border-radius:2px; }
  .handoff h3{ font-family:'Fraunces',serif; font-weight:600; font-size:clamp(16px,1.8vw,19px);
    line-height:1.35; color:var(--ink); margin:0 0 7px; }
  .handoff p{ color:var(--soft); font-size:15.5px; line-height:1.7; max-width:52ch; margin:0 0 12px; }
  .handoff a{ font-family:'Work Sans',sans-serif; font-size:14px; font-weight:500;
    letter-spacing:.02em; color:var(--accent); text-decoration:none;
    border-bottom:1px solid rgba(79,107,74,.35); padding-bottom:2px; transition:border-color .3s ease; }
  .handoff a:hover{ border-color:var(--accent); }
  @media(max-width:720px){ .handoff{ padding:18px 18px 20px; } }

  .note{ margin-top:30px; font-size:15.5px; line-height:1.75; color:var(--soft);
    max-width:60ch; }

/* ---- DISC-008 experiment v2 — before / possible comparison.
     Quieter control, direct pointer relationship, no easing on the divider.
     Inherits .imagine-photo for full-bleed, height and section rhythm.
     Controls appear only once .is-live is set by script. ---- */
  .cmp{ --pos:65%; touch-action:pan-y; -webkit-user-select:none; user-select:none; }
  .cmp img{ position:absolute; inset:0; -webkit-user-drag:none; user-drag:none; }
  .cmp img.cmp-over{ display:none; }   /* must outrank .imagine-photo img{display:block} */
  .cmp-divider,.cmp-tag,.cmp-range{ display:none; }

  .cmp.is-live{ cursor:ew-resize; }
  .cmp.is-live .cmp-over{
    display:block;
    clip-path:inset(0 calc(100% - var(--pos)) 0 0);
  }

  /* hairline: ivory, with the faintest dark edge so it survives both images */
  .cmp.is-live .cmp-divider{
    display:block; position:absolute; top:0; bottom:0; z-index:4;
    left:var(--pos); width:1px; margin-left:-0.5px;
    background:rgba(248,245,236,.72);
    box-shadow:0 0 0 0.5px rgba(15,14,10,.16);
    pointer-events:none;
  }

  /* handle: 44px hit box, 26px visible ring, no disc, no shadow */
  .cmp.is-live .cmp-handle{
    position:absolute; top:50%; left:50%;
    width:44px; height:44px; margin:-22px 0 0 -22px;
    display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:center;
  }
  .cmp.is-live .cmp-handle::before{
    content:''; width:30px; height:30px; border-radius:50%;
    border:1px solid rgba(248,245,236,.78);
    background:rgba(15,14,10,.06);
  }
  .cmp.is-live .cmp-chev{
    position:absolute; top:50%; width:4px; height:4px;
    border-top:1px solid rgba(248,245,236,.85);
    border-right:1px solid rgba(248,245,236,.85);
  }
  .cmp.is-live .cmp-chev-l{ left:12px; transform:translateY(-50%) rotate(-135deg); }
  .cmp.is-live .cmp-chev-r{ right:12px; transform:translateY(-50%) rotate(45deg); }

  /* labels: lower corners, out of the caption's way */

    display:block; position:absolute; bottom:3.2vh; z-index:4;

  /* ---- THE DECISION BOARD (DISC-014). Composition, materiality, hierarchy.
     Existing tokens only: --paper, --cream, --ink, --soft, --accent,
     Fraunces, Work Sans, tints of the brand green.

     HIERARCHY BY SURFACE COUNT, not by shadow weight. Qualification and
     advisory are SETS OF TILES -- discrete objects you could pick up. The
     earnings feature is the one UNBROKEN surface, and the only one that
     dominates. Elevation supports that reading rather than carrying it:
       earnings 64px  >  advisory tiles 26px  >  qualification tiles 20px
       >  evidence drawers 16px

     Type roles are shared across every zone so the board stays one object:
       .dq-cat  Work Sans 9.5px/.24em/--accent   .dq-fact Fraunces/--ink
       .dq-note Work Sans/--soft ---- */

  /* 1 · QUALIFICATION — three tactile tiles under one editorial rule. The
     rule spans the whole stage, so they still read as one qualification step
     rather than three unrelated cards. */
  .dq-qual{ list-style:none; margin:32px 0 0; padding:14px 0 0;
    display:grid; grid-template-columns:repeat(3,1fr); gap:10px;
    border-top:2px solid rgba(31,59,46,.55); background:none;
    border-left:none; border-right:none; border-bottom:none;
    box-shadow:none; border-radius:0; }
  .dq-qual > li{ margin:0; padding:20px 22px 22px;
    background:var(--paper); border:1px solid rgba(31,59,46,.09);
    border-top:1px solid rgba(31,59,46,.22); border-radius:2px;
    box-shadow:0 1px 2px rgba(31,59,46,.05),
               0 10px 20px -14px rgba(31,59,46,.32); }
  .dq-qual > li:first-child{ padding-left:22px; }
  .dq-qual > li:not(:first-child){ padding-left:22px; }

  .dq-cat{ display:block; font-family:'Work Sans',sans-serif; font-size:9.5px;
    font-weight:500; letter-spacing:.24em; text-transform:uppercase;
    color:var(--accent); margin-bottom:12px; }
  .dq-fact{ display:block; font-family:'Fraunces',Georgia,serif;
    font-weight:500; font-size:16px; line-height:1.34; color:var(--ink); }
  .dq-note{ display:block; font-family:'Work Sans',sans-serif; margin-top:8px;
    font-size:12.5px; line-height:1.7; color:var(--soft); }

  /* 2 · OPPORTUNITY — the one unbroken surface, and the highest. */
  .dq-opp{ margin-top:40px; display:grid; grid-template-columns:1.62fr 1fr;
    gap:1px; background:rgba(31,59,46,.15);
    border:1px solid rgba(31,59,46,.15);
    border-top:2px solid rgba(31,59,46,.55); border-radius:2px;
    box-shadow:0 2px 4px rgba(31,59,46,.07),
               0 30px 64px -30px rgba(31,59,46,.42); }
  .dq-earn{ background:var(--paper); padding:40px 42px 44px; }
  .dq-use{ background:var(--cream); padding:36px 30px 40px;
    box-shadow:inset 1px 0 0 rgba(255,255,255,.5); }

  .dq-earn-lead{ font-family:'Fraunces',Georgia,serif; font-weight:500;
    font-size:19px; line-height:1.32; color:var(--ink); margin:0; }
  .dq-earn-caveat{ font-family:'Work Sans',sans-serif; font-size:12.5px;
    line-height:1.7; color:var(--soft); margin:10px 0 0; max-width:46ch; }

  /* the two reported examples: separated by a rule, with real air around
     them. Never boxed -- boxing them would make them price cards. */
  .dq-figs{ list-style:none; margin:40px 0 4px; padding:0;
    display:grid; grid-template-columns:repeat(2,1fr); gap:0; }
  .dq-figs > li{ margin:0; padding:26px 30px 4px 0;
    border-top:1px solid rgba(31,59,46,.22); }

    letter-spacing:-.022em; color:var(--ink); }
  .dq-src{ display:block; font-family:'Work Sans',sans-serif; margin-top:14px;
    font-size:12px; line-height:1.6; color:var(--soft); max-width:30ch; }

  /* the mechanism steps down in type as well as width */
  .dq-rows{ list-style:none; margin:16px 0 0; padding:0; }
  .dq-rows > li{ margin:16px 0 0; padding-top:16px;
    border-top:1px solid rgba(31,59,46,.12); }
  .dq-rows > li:first-child{ margin-top:0; padding-top:0; border-top:none; }
  .dq-use .dq-fact{ font-size:15px; }
  .dq-use .dq-note{ font-size:12px; }

  /* 3 · ADVISORY — three floating tiles, calm and clearly subordinate. */
  .dq-adv{ margin-top:40px; background:none; border:none; border-radius:0;
    padding:14px 0 0; border-top:2px solid rgba(31,59,46,.42);
    box-shadow:none; }
  .dq-adv-cat{ margin-bottom:16px; color:var(--soft); }
  .dq-adv-cols{ list-style:none; margin:0; padding:0;
    display:grid; grid-template-columns:repeat(3,1fr); gap:10px; }
  .dq-adv-cols > li{ margin:0; padding:22px 24px 24px;
    background:var(--cream); border:1px solid rgba(31,59,46,.11);
    border-top:1px solid rgba(31,59,46,.26); border-radius:2px;
    box-shadow:0 1px 2px rgba(31,59,46,.06),
               0 14px 26px -16px rgba(31,59,46,.34); }
  .dq-adv-cols > li:first-child{ padding-left:24px; }
  .dq-adv-label{ display:block; font-family:'Work Sans',sans-serif;
    font-size:9.5px; font-weight:500; letter-spacing:.22em;
    text-transform:uppercase; color:var(--accent); margin-bottom:10px; }
  .dq-adv .dq-fact{ font-size:15px; }

  /* MOTION — pointer devices only; tiles lift individually, the feature
     lifts as one object. */
  @media (hover:hover) and (pointer:fine){
    .dq-qual > li, .dq-opp, .dq-adv-cols > li{

  /* ---- THE EVIDENCE LAYER (DISC-014). Native details/summary, unchanged

Above and Beyond

Imagine if your garden had a second level.

Illustrative AI-generated visualisation. Not an actual installation.
blocks: Look up
Stand at the back door and look at your garden. You are almost certainly measuring the ground.
Everyone thinks about garden space as a footprint — so much lawn, so much patio. A new room has to come out of it, so building something means the garden gets smaller.
Now look up.
The space above the lawn is already yours, and it rarely gets counted. What if the extra space was above it?
People build up there, in Ireland, in ordinary gardens, including small ones. You can buy one this week. And the thing that decides what you end up with is not the thing you would expect.
You don’t need a tree
A treehouse without a tree sounds like a contradiction, and it isn’t. A structure can bring its own support — posts, stilts, columns or an engineered frame — and stand up entirely on its own.

Irish and British builders describe the category that way themselves, and Irish suppliers sell it by name — a playhouse on stilts, with a ladder, a swing, and decking under . The decking under is the part worth noticing.
The moment a suitable tree stops being a requirement, the idea opens up to gardens where a traditional treehouse would not work.
There are three ways one of these can stand up.
Three ways the same deck can stand
Tree-supported
The tree carries the load.
Tree-supported The tree carries the load.
Part-supported
The tree and posts share it.
Part-supported The tree and posts share it.
Freestanding
Posts carry it. No tree at all.
Freestanding Posts carry it. No tree at all.
The deck is drawn at the same height in all three. Only the support changes, which is the whole point: the thing that matters to the regulations is how high it is, not what is holding it up.
Freestanding
The structure stands on its own supports, so no suitable tree is required.
Part tree, part support
A tree forms part of the structure, with additional engineered support carrying the rest. Common where there is a good tree, but not one that can do the whole job alone.
Tree-supported
The traditional version, where suitable trees form part of the support. It depends entirely on having the right tree in the right place.
Which route works depends on the garden, the structure and what you want to use it for. The important point is that a suitable tree is not a requirement.
What it can become
This is where people underestimate it. The picture in most heads is a small timber box for small children, outgrown in about three summers.
It does not have to be that. Laid end to end, the published work runs from a den a metre off the lawn to something an architect signs.
A raised den
A platform, a ladder or steps, a small enclosed space and a veranda. This is the volume product, and it is where most Irish gardens start.
A play and adventure structure
Towers, slides, monkey bars, climbing walls, nets, crow’s nests. Irish makers publish bridges between towers, drop bridges and in-ground trampolines at this level, not only at the ambitious end.
A substantial elevated room

Enclosed, boarded, glazed. One Irish maker’s published Dublin project is a games room treehouse, elevated and built around a mature birch to give a sense of being in the canopy while avoiding overlook of neighbouring gardens.
An adult retreat

The same maker publishes a County Louth retreat in a mature oak with a wrap-around deck that lets you follow the sun, and says that depending on the comfort level required these can be fully insulated and heated for year-round use.
A games room, studio or workspace

At the frontier these are published as standing product lines — studios, home offices, garden rooms in the air. In Ireland the games room is the evidenced example. If you would rather keep it at ground level, see what garden rooms cost in Ireland .
An architectural treehouse

The most ambitious published example built in Ireland is on the Atlantic coast: a look-out deck, a rope bridge, a reading nook, cedar cladding and a glass window in the floor, designed for a windy, exposed site. It was built by a British practice, and whether that practice currently takes on private commissions here is something PlotNua has not established.
PlotNua concept image — an imagined direction, not a photographed supplier project.

One important distinction. This is not something anyone sells off a shelf. It is not a standard Irish product, it would not suit every garden, and nothing about a structure this size should be assumed to be exempted development.

Not every structure suits every use, and the use changes what has to be built. Insulation, power, glazing, how you get up there and how often you go — somewhere to read on a June evening and somewhere to work in February are different briefs.

How we got these figures

Between €4,100 and €30,000 no Irish supplier we found publishes a price. Quote-only makers may well work in that band — at least one Irish maker offers a free approximate estimate online rather than a price list. What we can say is narrower and more useful: no published Irish price establishes that band. PlotNua does not fill it with a guess, and we will not borrow one from another market to make the picture look complete. All figures read first-party on the supplier’s own website on 5 October 2026.

Planning rules are a big reason.

The exemption limit

The exemption for a structure of this kind sets a limit of 3 metres, measured overall from ground level to the highest point, and allows 4 metres only where the roof is a tiled or slated pitched roof. The two conditions hold together: a felted or shingled roof at any pitch is on the 3 metre line, which is why quoting the higher figure on its own would be the most misleading thing this page could do.
What Irish suppliers actually publish

Timbertrove publish the only complete measured elevation we found in Ireland — a deck at 1.2 metres, 2.7 metres overall, felted roof — for the Hide Out Treehouse at €2,339. Geppetto Land and Garden Sheds Dublin each publish deck heights of about 4 feet for products in their ranges. No Irish catalogue product we found is published with a tiled or slated pitched roof, so in practice the ready-made market is working to the 3 metre figure.
Where Class 3 stops
Class 3 of the exempted-development regulations does not name treehouses, and this page does not assert that any particular structure is within it.
How to get an answer that binds

Under section 5 of the Planning and Development Act 2000 any person can ask their planning authority for a declaration on whether something is development and whether it is exempted development. That is the only binding answer available.

The two classes

Class 3 covers garden structures of this kind and counts every one in the curtilage together. Since July 2026 a separate class has allowed a small detached house in a back garden without planning permission, for a limited period, where it is occupied along with the main house. They are different exemptions, and they share an overall area ceiling.
The arithmetic, and whose it is

The combined ceiling across both classes is 45 square metres. A detached garden house has a floor it cannot go below of 32 square metres. Taken together that leaves about 13 square metres — roughly a three-by-four-metre building plus a modest deck — for garden structures of this kind before the garden house route closes. That reading is PlotNua’s own, drawn from two sets of regulations, and it is not guidance from any authority. We set it out so you can check it rather than take it.
What to do about it

If a garden house is anywhere in your thinking, put the question to your local authority before you order a treehouse rather than after. A section 5 declaration is the way to get an answer that binds.

Eleven treehouses in native Irish timber, from Wicklow. They are the only supplier we found who puts free nationwide delivery and assembly inside every published price.

These specialists show some of the directions treehouse design has taken beyond Ireland — from freestanding structures to adult spaces and architecture designed around individual trees.

A practice in East Sussex whose Wild Atlantic Treehouse was built on the Irish coast: a look-out deck, a rope bridge, a reading nook and a glass window in the floor, designed for a windy, exposed site. Surrey, and more than a hundred treehouses over twenty years. They give the flattest answer anywhere to the tree question — no you don’t — and say they have built many without trees with nothing lacking in the result. Ireland is not one of their offices and is not among their published projects.
baumraum

A Bremen architecture practice that has kept Stelzenhäuser — stilt houses — as a standing category for over twenty years, for children and adults alike, from small play spaces to fully habitable ones. Ireland is not among their published projects.

Bristol. They scan the tree: reality-capture technology imports its actual geometry into the design software, so the design is drawn to the tree rather than around an assumption. A free consultation and design visit come first, and the design is presented as a 3D model. Ireland is not established as a service area.

They publish a page headed you don’t need a tree to have a treehouse , and will build freestanding on stilts in gardens, fields or by rivers. Adult uses include home offices and insulated year-round rooms, with builds of about four to eight weeks after the design is agreed. Ireland is not established as a service area.

The height limit, and why it is usually three metres
The planning rule
The 4-metre allowance in Class 3 is conditional on a tiled or slated pitched roof.
Any other covering falls under any other case and the limit is 3 metres.
What Irish suppliers publish
The coverings Irish makers publish are mineral felt, shingles and steel sheeting, including a slate-effect steel.
A slate-effect finish is not slate.
Building Regulations are a separate regime

A separate regime, worded differently. The Building Regulations are a separate regime from planning, administered by your local Building Control Authority rather than the planning section, and the two area figures are not the same .

Building Regulations 1997, S.I. No. 497 of 1997, Article 8 and the Third Schedule exempt a single storey building ancillary to a dwelling: detached, not more than 25 square metres, used exclusively for recreational or storage purposes and not for any trade or business, and no human habitation.
Height limit 3 metres, or — for a building with a pitched roof, and unlike the planning condition, with no requirement that it be tiled or slated — 4 metres.
The two regimes also use different area figures: planning now allows 30 square metres, the Building Regulations exemption is 25 square metres.
What this means
So the binding constraint on height is planning, not building control.
What the planning rules actually say — read directly

Class 3, as substituted by S.I. No. 338 of 2026 , in force 27 July 2026. It permits the construction, erection or placing within the curtilage of a house of any tent, awning, shade or other object, greenhouse, garage, store, shed or other similar structure, subject to six conditions:
nothing forward of the front wall of the house;
a combined floor area for all such structures of no more than 30 square metres;
no reduction of private open space to the rear or side below 25 square metres;
external finishes, and the roof covering where the roof is tiled or slated, to conform with those of the house for anything placed to the side;
a height limit of 4 metres for a structure with a tiled or slated pitched roof and 3 metres in any other case;
and no human habitation, and no use for any purpose other than one incidental to the enjoyment of the house.
The area figure changed
The previous limit was 25 square metres; the 2026 substitution raised it to 30. Both are stated here because older guidance carries the old one.
What Class 3 does not say
Class 3 does not name treehouses, playhouses, play towers or elevated structures. Whether a raised structure is read that way is not something PlotNua could establish.

Space: what counts, and what has to be left
Space: what counts, and what has to be left
Why the limit is about the whole garden rather than one structure, and where the two classes meet.
It all adds up, across the whole garden

Class 3 counts every structure of this kind in the curtilage together, not one at a time. The combined total must not exceed 30 square metres. The previous limit was 25 square metres and a lot of guidance still says so, which is worth knowing if you are reading something older.
You have to leave open space behind
The same class says the structure must not reduce the private open space to the rear or side of the house below 25 square metres. On a small plot this bites before the area limit does.
Where it sits changes the specification

Nothing of this kind may go forward of the front wall of the house. And anything placed to the side of the house must have external finishes — and, where it has a tiled or slated roof, a roof covering — that conform with those of the house. A side-garden structure is not simply a rear-garden one moved over.
The detached garden house, and how it interacts
What the class permits
A separate class inserted in July 2026.
It permits a detached house in the rear garden of a principal house, for a period ending 31 December 2030, occupied only in conjunction with the main dwelling and not sold or subdivided separately.
Building control legislation including fire safety applies.
A notification must reach the planning authority not less than fourteen days before works commence.
It requires a floor area of not less than 32 square metres.
It caps that area, taken together with any structures previously placed under Class 3 in the same curtilage, at 45 square metres.

The consequence set out in this page is PlotNua’s reading of those two provisions together, not guidance from any authority. Build more than about thirteen square metres of garden structures and what remains of the 45 falls below the 32-square-metre floor.
The Class 3A arithmetic in full, and whose reading it is
What the separate route allows
Since July 2026 there is a separate route, a different class from the one that covers garden structures, and it comes with its own conditions.
It lets you put a whole small detached house in your back garden without planning permission, for a limited period, if it is occupied in conjunction with the main house.
Building regulations including fire safety apply.
You have to notify the council fourteen days before you start.
The catch: two numbers that interact
That route requires the house to be at least 32 square metres.
And it caps the house, taken together with the garden structures already built under the garden-structure class, at 45 square metres combined.

So the two interact. The more garden structure you build now, the less garden house is available later. Past roughly thirteen square metres of structures, what remains falls below the 32-square-metre floor and that route closes. This is PlotNua’s reading of two sets of regulations, not guidance from any authority. The arithmetic is ours.
For scale
A small treehouse deck is around four square metres.
A three-by-four-metre structure is twelve.

So you can usually have both — but only if somebody counts, and nobody is going to count for you at the point of sale. If a garden house is anywhere in your thinking, it is worth putting to your local authority before you order a treehouse, not after.

The tree is a specialist question, and not the one you expect
How builders attach to a tree — two published methods
One builder guarantees never to damage the tree, because the structure is not attached to it at all.
The standard alternative uses an engineered bolt that lets the tree keep moving and growing.
Either way, branch removal goes to a professional tree surgeon.

The counter-intuitive part: the risk is in the ground

For a freestanding structure near a tree, the arboricultural risk sits mostly in the footings, the excavation and where the materials get stacked, because all of that happens inside the root protection area. Your instinct will be to worry about bolts. The standard worries about the ground. That is PlotNua’s reading of the professional guidance, which is a British Standard rather than an Irish legal requirement.
Tree Preservation Orders

A planning authority can make a Tree Preservation Order under section 205 of the Planning and Development Act 2000, which can prohibit the cutting down, topping, lopping or wilful destruction of the trees it names. Contravening one, or even a proposed one, is an offence.

Attaching something is not in that list, but an individual order can carry its own conditions, so the order has to be read. Whether a TPO also restricts attaching a structure to a tree is not something PlotNua could establish.
Getting up there takes ground, and so does the space around it
Access is a design problem, not an afterthought. Steps, a ladder, a bridge or some combination, and all of them take up ground.
The only published figures for clear space
A cushioned surface extending at least 6 feet past the equipment.
Loose fill 12 inches deep for equipment up to 8 feet high.

That is one Irish supplier’s own practice, published as fall-zone guidance for its own range, expressed in feet and inches and evidently drawn from public-playground guidance. It is not an Irish requirement and nothing here presents it as one. It is still the most concrete answer anyone publishes to how much room you actually need around the thing.
What nobody should tell you

Nobody should tell you an elevated structure costs you no garden at all. Supports, access, foundations and the clear space around it all take some. The more accurate claim is that much of the garden underneath and around it can stay useful — and one Irish supplier sells exactly that, a playhouse on stilts with decking underneath.
Safety standards are a commitment, not a requirement

EN 1176, the European playground equipment standard, covers permanently installed equipment in public and shared settings — parks, schools, housing estates. Equipment intended for private family use at a single home falls outside its scope, so it is not a mandatory domestic requirement, and nothing here is presented as certified to it. If a builder tells you a structure meets a European safety standard, that is a commitment they have chosen to make. It is a good question to ask and a good answer to get.

Your own policy
The CCPC notes that buildings cover usually includes outbuildings such as a garden shed.
You may need to increase your cover if you extend or improve your home.

The CCPC says damage caused by someone working in your home is not usually covered by your own buildings policy.
You can only claim if the person who caused it has their own public liability insurance.
The CCPC says, twice, to check that anyone working on your home has it. So ask for the certificates and keep them.

Trees, standards and insurance
Tree Preservation Orders

Section 205, Planning and Development Act 2000. A planning authority may make a Tree Preservation Order in the interests of amenity or the environment; it is a reserved function of the elected members.
An order may prohibit the cutting down, topping, lopping or wilful destruction of the trees it names, and contravening an order, or a proposed order pending decision, is an offence.
Attachment is not among the prohibitions the Act names, but an order may carry its own conditions.
Whether a TPO also restricts attaching a structure to a tree is not something PlotNua could establish.
Root protection

The professional framework for trees near construction is a British Standard rather than an Irish legal requirement. It calculates a root protection area at design stage, within which ground disturbance, excavation, trenching, utility installation and material storage should not occur. PlotNua’s inference that footings matter more than fixings for a freestanding structure follows from that, and is labelled as inference.
EN 1176 is the European standard for playground equipment.
Published scope descriptions state that it covers permanently installed public playground equipment and excludes items defined as toys in EN 71.
Equipment intended for private family use at a single home falls outside it.
The standard text itself sits behind a paywall and was not read; this is a catalogue scope statement, not a reading of the standard.
It is not a mandatory domestic requirement and nothing on this page is presented as certified to it.
Insurance
The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission, the statutory Irish consumer body, states:
that buildings cover usually includes garages or outbuildings such as a garden shed;
that if you extend or improve your home you may need to increase your buildings cover;
that standard exclusions are in every policy but specific exclusions vary and should always be checked;
that damage caused by someone working in your home is not usually covered and can only be claimed where that person has their own public liability insurance;
and, as a tip, to always check that anyone working on your home has it.

Exemption can disappear for reasons that have nothing to do with size

Article 9 of the same regulations removes exempted-development status in a list of circumstances: contravening a condition of an existing permission, interfering with a view or prospect of special amenity value protected by the development plan, obstructing a public right of way, works in an architectural conservation area that would materially affect its character, or extending an unauthorised structure. Class 3 is also named specifically: in an area covered by a special amenity area order it is not exempted development at all. If the house is a protected structure, or in a conservation area, the route is a Section 57 Declaration rather than a Section 5.
The way to get an actual answer
Under section 5 of the Planning and Development Act 2000 any person can ask their planning authority for a declaration on whether something is development, and whether it is exempted development.
The authority must issue the declaration and the main reasons for it within four weeks, or within three weeks of receiving any further information it asks for.
The fee in the county whose register we read is €80, payable to the planning authority.
The application needs the relevant site maps.
Two things worth knowing before you apply
A Section 5 considers only whether something is development and whether it is exempt — no planning policy, no design view.
The question has to be posed clearly or the application comes back invalid, which is the most common way people lose a month.
Getting a binding answer, and one real case
The statutory route

Under section 5 of the Planning and Development Act 2000 any person may, on payment of the prescribed fee, request a declaration from the planning authority on whether something is or is not development, and is or is not exempted development.
The authority must issue the declaration and the main reasons and considerations within four weeks, or within three weeks of receiving requested further information.
A declaration may be referred for review within four weeks of issue.
Details of every declaration are entered in a public register, which is why the case below is readable.
The fee in the register we read is €80, set by that planning authority, and the application requires the relevant site maps.
A Section 5 considers only development and exemption; no planning policy is considered.
An unclear question is returned invalid.
The case

Louth County Council’s 2025 register records a request asking whether a recently erected playroom structure in the rear of a property was development and was exempted development. The decision was a refusal. The register gives no reasons, no dimensions, and does not say whether the structure was elevated. It is one declaration by one authority and it is not a rule that binds others. Read first-party, 5 October 2026.
One real Irish case, and what it does not tell you

In 2025 a homeowner in County Louth asked the council whether a recently erected playroom structure in the rear of a property was development, and whether it was exempted development. The council refused the declaration. Read that carefully, because it is thinner than it looks. The public register records the question and the decision but not the reasons, and it says nothing about the structure’s dimensions or whether it was elevated at all. It is one case, decided by one authority, and it is not a rule that binds anybody else. What it does show is that this question reaches councils, and that already having built the thing does not settle it.

The site conditions that decide more than the regulations do.
Slope and access decide more than they should

One supplier’s floor height varies with the slope of the garden. Another supplies levelling blocks on the condition that the site is clear and level. A third publishes a site and access requirements page, because getting the materials down the side of a house is the classic lost day. Re-levelling is itself a planning question. In one published Louth case a proposal to raise and lower rear-garden ground levels by no more than a metre was refused exempted-development status.
Light and overlooking are design questions, not rules

Class 3 itself contains no window-to-boundary condition, so this is not something the regulations decide for you. It is still real. One Irish maker’s published Dublin project was deliberately elevated to sit in the canopy while avoiding overlook of neighbouring gardens. Another tells customers plainly that the bigger tree houses would not suit a smaller garden because they may block views and a lot of sunlight. That is a supplier talking someone out of the larger model, which is worth more than a brochure.
